title: Metronidazole and Alcohol: The 72-Hour Rule and What Happens
excerpt: Can you drink on metronidazole (Flagyl)? Why the label says no alcohol for 72 hours, what the research really shows about the reaction, hidden alcohol sources, and what to do if you slipped up.
metaDescription: Can you drink on metronidazole (Flagyl)? The 72-hour rule, what the reaction feels like, hidden alcohol in mouthwash, and what to do if you already drank.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't drink alcohol while you're taking metronidazole (brand name Flagyl), and wait at least 72 hours (three full days) after your last dose before you have a drink. That's what the official prescribing information says, and it's what almost every doctor and pharmacist will tell you. The reason is what the drug label calls a **disulfiram-like reaction** (similar to what the alcohol-deterrent drug Antabuse causes), which can bring on flushing, a pounding headache, nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and a racing heart. The science behind that reaction turns out to be shakier than most articles admit, and we'll walk through it honestly below. But "the evidence is mixed" is not the same as "it's safe," and the cost of waiting a few days is small compared with spending a night vomiting while you're trying to get over an infection.

**The quick rules:** No alcohol from your first pill until 72 hours after your last one. That includes the "sneaky" sources: alcohol-based mouthwash, liquid cold and cough medicines, kombucha, and anything else that lists alcohol, ethanol, or propylene glycol on the label. If you accidentally drank, don't panic and don't skip your next dose. Most reactions, if they happen at all, are unpleasant but pass within a few hours. Call your pharmacist for advice, and get emergency care if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or vomiting you can't stop.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and why you were prescribed metronidazole. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist** before drinking any alcohol during or shortly after treatment, before stopping your antibiotic early, and if you take disulfiram (Antabuse), warfarin or another blood thinner, lithium, or any other regular medicine. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you develop chest pain, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, or severe vomiting after drinking on metronidazole.

## Why Metronidazole and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Metronidazole is an antibiotic and anti-parasite drug. It's prescribed for a long list of common infections: bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, some dental and gum infections, certain stomach and gut infections (including *C. difficile* and as part of some *H. pylori* treatments), giardia, and infections after surgery. It works well against bacteria that live without oxygen and against some parasites. It's cheap, effective, and widely used.

It also comes with one of the best-known alcohol warnings in medicine. The official US prescribing information for oral metronidazole says that using it with alcohol has been associated with a **"disulfiram-like reaction."** That phrase needs unpacking.

### What "disulfiram-like" means

Disulfiram (brand name Antabuse) is a drug that some people take on purpose to make drinking unpleasant. Here's how it works. When you drink, your liver breaks alcohol down in two steps:

1. **Alcohol becomes acetaldehyde.** Acetaldehyde is a toxic, irritating chemical. It's a big part of why heavy drinking makes people feel sick, and it's the same chemical behind the facial flushing some people get from even a small drink.
2. **Acetaldehyde becomes acetate.** An enzyme called aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) turns acetaldehyde into acetate, which is harmless and eventually becomes carbon dioxide and water.

Disulfiram blocks that second step. Acetaldehyde piles up in the blood, and within minutes of drinking the person gets hot and red in the face, their heart pounds, their head throbs, and they feel sick and often vomit.

When doctors started seeing patients on metronidazole get sick after drinking, the natural explanation was that metronidazole must be doing the same thing: blocking ALDH and letting acetaldehyde build up. That's where the "disulfiram-like" label came from, and it's the explanation you'll still read on most websites.

### The symptoms people report

The reaction described on the label and in case reports includes:

- Flushing (a hot, red face and neck)
- Throbbing headache
- Nausea and vomiting
- Stomach cramps or abdominal pain
- A fast or pounding heartbeat
- Sweating
- Feeling dizzy or short of breath

In most reported cases these symptoms are unpleasant but short-lived. In rare case reports, people have had more serious problems, such as a dangerous drop in blood pressure or heart rhythm trouble. Those serious cases are the reason the warning is taken seriously even though they're uncommon.

## Is the Metronidazole Alcohol Reaction a Myth?

This is the question a lot of people search for, and it deserves a straight answer. **The evidence for the reaction is weaker than most people assume, but it is not a myth you should test on yourself.**

### What the skeptics point to

A few things have made researchers question the classic story:

- **The mechanism hasn't held up well.** In animal and lab work, researchers have struggled to show that metronidazole blocks liver ALDH in the way disulfiram does.
- **A small controlled trial didn't find it.** A placebo-controlled study from Finland, published in *Annals of Pharmacotherapy* in 2002 (Visapää and colleagues), gave healthy volunteers metronidazole or a placebo and then a dose of alcohol. The researchers didn't find higher acetaldehyde levels or the classic reaction in the metronidazole group. It was a small study in healthy young men, so it can't rule out reactions in everyone, but it's the best direct test we have.
- **Reviews of the case reports are underwhelming.** A review in the same journal in 2000 (Williams and Woodcock) looked back at the published reports and concluded that the evidence for a true disulfiram-like interaction was weak. Many reports were old, had few details, or involved people who were already sick, which makes it hard to tell what caused the symptoms.
- **Metronidazole causes similar symptoms on its own.** Nausea, a metallic taste, headache, and stomach upset are common side effects of the drug even if you never touch alcohol. So is the infection you're treating. If someone has a drink and then feels sick, it's genuinely hard to say whether the alcohol, the antibiotic, or the illness was to blame.

### Why doctors still say no alcohol

Even with those doubts, the official guidance hasn't changed, and there are good reasons for that:

- **"Not found in a small study" isn't "proven safe."** The trial tested a limited group of healthy people under controlled conditions. It doesn't tell you how you'll react, especially if you're older, sick, taking other medicines, or drinking more than a single measured dose.
- **Case reports keep appearing.** Some people do seem to get the full flushing, vomiting, and pounding-heart picture after drinking on metronidazole. Other mechanisms have been suggested, but nobody has settled why it happens in some people and not others. Not knowing the cause makes it impossible to predict who's at risk.
- **Alcohol makes the side effects worse anyway.** Even with no special reaction at all, alcohol irritates the stomach, dehydrates you, and disrupts sleep. Stacking that on top of an antibiotic that already causes nausea, while your body is fighting an infection, is a recipe for feeling awful.
- **The downside of waiting is tiny.** Most courses of metronidazole last somewhere between a single dose and two weeks. Skipping drinks for that time plus three days is a small price compared with the risk of a rough reaction or a worse recovery.

So the honest summary is: the reaction may be less common and less predictable than the textbooks once claimed, but no one can tell you that *you* won't get it. The label still says avoid alcohol, and that's the advice to follow.

## How Long After Metronidazole Can You Drink? The 72-Hour Rule

The US prescribing information for oral metronidazole tells people to avoid alcohol and products containing propylene glycol **during treatment and for at least three days afterward.** That's where the "72-hour rule" comes from.

### Why three days?

It's about how long the drug stays in your body. Metronidazole has a half-life of roughly eight hours in healthy adults, meaning the amount in your blood drops by about half every eight hours. It usually takes around five half-lives for a drug to be mostly cleared, which works out to roughly 40 hours. The 72-hour window adds a comfortable safety margin on top of that, partly because clearance can be slower in some people, including older adults and people with liver problems.

A few practical points:

- **Count from your last pill, not your first.** If you finish a seven-day course on Sunday morning, the earliest you should consider a drink is Wednesday morning.
- **A single big dose still counts.** Some infections, such as trichomoniasis, are sometimes treated with one large dose. The 72-hour wait applies after that single dose too.
- **If you have liver disease, ask.** Metronidazole is cleared mainly by the liver, so if your liver doesn't work normally, the drug can hang around longer. Your doctor may suggest waiting longer.
- **Ease back in.** When the three days are up, start with one drink and see how you feel. You've just had an infection, and your gut may still be recovering from the antibiotic.

### What about tinidazole?

Tinidazole (brand name Tindamax) is a close relative of metronidazole that's used for many of the same infections. Its label carries the same kind of alcohol warning and the same advice to avoid alcohol during treatment and for three days afterward. If you've been switched from one to the other, the same rules apply.

## Flagyl and Alcohol: Is the Brand Any Different?

No. Flagyl is simply a brand name for metronidazole. Generic metronidazole tablets contain the same active drug and carry the same alcohol warning. Whatever the name on your pharmacy bag, the advice is identical: no alcohol during the course and for at least 72 hours after.

You may also see metronidazole combined with other drugs in a single package, such as some *H. pylori* treatment packs that bundle it with other antibiotics and a stomach-acid reducer. The alcohol warning still applies to those combination packs, and the other medicines in the pack may have their own instructions.

## Hidden Alcohol: Mouthwash, Cough Syrup, and Other Sneaky Sources

This is where people trip up most often. You can avoid beer and wine perfectly and still get alcohol from places you never think about. Because nobody knows exactly how much alcohol it takes to trigger a reaction in a sensitive person, the usual advice is to avoid these during treatment too, or at least ask your pharmacist about them.

### Mouthwash

Many popular mouthwashes contain a significant amount of alcohol. You don't swallow it on purpose, but some gets absorbed through your mouth and some gets swallowed. There are case reports of people reacting after using alcohol-based mouthwash on metronidazole. The easy fix is to switch to an alcohol-free mouthwash for the length of your course and three days after. This is especially relevant if you're taking metronidazole for a dental infection, since that's exactly when you'd be reaching for mouthwash.

### Liquid cold, cough, and flu medicines

Some liquid cold and cough medicines contain alcohol as a solvent. NyQuil's original liquid is a well-known example. If you're sick enough to need an antibiotic, you might also be reaching for cold medicine, so check the inactive ingredients. Tablets, capsules, and alcohol-free versions are usually available. Our guide to [cough medicine and alcohol](/never-hungover/cough-medicine-and-alcohol) explains which ingredients to watch for.

### Propylene glycol

The metronidazole label specifically mentions propylene glycol alongside alcohol. Propylene glycol is a common additive used to dissolve or stabilize ingredients in some liquid medicines, some foods, and some skin products. It's not the same as drinking alcohol, but the label groups them together, so it's worth asking your pharmacist if you take any liquid medicines during treatment.

### Food and drink you might not suspect

- **Kombucha.** It's fermented, and many brands contain small amounts of alcohol, sometimes more than the label suggests.
- **"Non-alcoholic" beer and wine.** In the US, these can legally contain up to 0.5% alcohol. That's a small amount, but it's not zero.
- **Cooking with wine, beer, or spirits.** Cooking doesn't burn off as much alcohol as people think, especially in sauces that simmer briefly or in desserts with liqueur. A splash in a long-cooked stew is probably minimal, but a boozy tiramisu or a flambé is a different story.
- **Vanilla and other extracts.** Pure vanilla extract is mostly alcohol by volume, though the amount used in baking is small.
- **Liquor-filled chocolates and boozy desserts.** Easy to forget about, easy to skip.

### What about hand sanitizer?

Hand sanitizer on your skin is generally not considered a problem. Very little alcohol gets through intact skin into your blood. Don't drink it, obviously, but you don't need to stop cleaning your hands.

## Metronidazole Gel and Alcohol

Metronidazole also comes as a gel or cream. There are two main types, and the answer is a little different for each.

### Topical gel or cream for the skin (rosacea)

Products like MetroGel, MetroCream, and generic metronidazole cream or gel are used on the face for rosacea. Very little of the drug gets into your bloodstream from skin use, so a reaction with alcohol is considered unlikely. Two things are worth knowing, though. First, alcohol is itself a common rosacea trigger, so drinking may make the redness you're treating worse. Second, if you have any doubt, your pharmacist can tell you what your specific product's label says.

### Vaginal gel (bacterial vaginosis)

Vaginal metronidazole gel is used to treat bacterial vaginosis. More of the drug is absorbed this way than from skin cream, though still much less than from pills. Labels for vaginal metronidazole products generally still mention the alcohol interaction seen with the oral drug and advise caution. The safest approach is to treat it like the tablets: avoid alcohol during treatment and for a few days after, and ask your pharmacist if you're unsure what your product's label says.

## I Accidentally Drank Alcohol on Metronidazole. What Now?

It happens. Someone hands you a glass of champagne at a party, you forget you're on antibiotics, or you only realize afterward that the cocktail sauce or the mouthwash had alcohol in it. Here's what to do.

### 1. Stop drinking and stay calm

Don't have any more. Many people who accidentally drink a small amount on metronidazole feel nothing unusual at all. If a reaction does happen, it usually starts within minutes to an hour or so of drinking and, in most reported cases, fades over the next few hours.

### 2. Watch for symptoms

The usual signs are flushing, a pounding headache, nausea, vomiting, cramps, sweating, and a fast heartbeat. If you feel any of these:

- Sit or lie down somewhere comfortable, ideally with someone nearby.
- Sip water slowly to stay hydrated, especially if you're vomiting.
- Avoid more alcohol, caffeine, and heavy food until you feel better.
- Don't take more medicine to "treat" it without checking with a pharmacist first.

### 3. Don't skip your next dose or stop the antibiotic

This is the most important point and the one people get wrong. Don't stop your metronidazole or skip doses to "make room" for drinking or to avoid a reaction. Stopping early can let the infection come back, and it can make the bacteria or parasites harder to treat next time. Call your pharmacist, explain what happened, and ask whether you should take your next dose on schedule. In most cases, the answer will be yes.

### 4. Call your pharmacist or doctor

A pharmacist can answer this kind of question quickly and for free. Tell them what you drank, how much, when, and how you feel. In the US, you can also call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** for free, confidential advice any time of day.

### When to get emergency care

Call 911 or go to the emergency room if you or someone with you has:

- Chest pain or tightness
- Trouble breathing or a feeling of choking
- A very fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle
- Fainting, or feeling like you're about to pass out
- Confusion, severe drowsiness, or being hard to wake
- Vomiting that won't stop, or vomiting blood
- Signs of a severe allergic reaction, such as swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or a widespread rash

These are uncommon, but they're the reason the warning exists. If you're unsure whether symptoms are serious, it's always fine to call for help.

## Who Should Be Especially Careful

Some people need extra caution with metronidazole, with or without alcohol:

- **Anyone who has taken disulfiram (Antabuse) recently.** The metronidazole label says it should not be used in people who have taken disulfiram within the last two weeks, because the combination has been linked to serious psychiatric reactions, including confusion and psychosis. Make sure your prescriber knows.
- **People taking warfarin or other blood thinners.** Metronidazole can boost the effect of warfarin and raise the risk of bleeding. Your doctor may want to check your blood more often. Alcohol also affects blood clotting, which adds another layer.
- **People taking lithium.** Metronidazole can raise lithium levels in the blood, so monitoring may be needed.
- **People with liver disease.** The drug is cleared mainly by the liver, so levels can build up. Your doctor may adjust your dose and may advise a longer alcohol-free window.
- **People with heart rhythm problems or low blood pressure.** If a reaction does happen, a racing heart and a drop in blood pressure are harder on people with existing heart conditions.
- **Anyone with nerve symptoms during treatment.** Numbness, tingling, or burning in the hands and feet, or unusual dizziness or clumsiness, can be side effects of metronidazole itself, especially with longer courses. Tell your doctor right away rather than waiting it out.

If you're pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor about both metronidazole and alcohol. That conversation is between you and your clinician.

## Other Antibiotics and Alcohol: Is Metronidazole Unusual?

Yes. It's one of a small number of antibiotics with a specific alcohol warning. For most common antibiotics, like amoxicillin and many others, there's no known direct chemical clash with moderate drinking, though doctors still often recommend skipping alcohol while you're sick so your body can recover. The main exceptions people should know about are:

- **Metronidazole and tinidazole**, covered above.
- **Certain cephalosporin antibiotics**, mainly some that are given in hospitals, have been linked to disulfiram-like reactions.
- **Some other antibiotics** have their own reasons for caution, such as effects on the liver or the way they're processed.

The simplest rule: whenever you're prescribed any antibiotic, ask the pharmacist, "Is there any problem with alcohol?" It takes ten seconds and they'll know the answer for your exact medicine.

## Can You Have Just One Drink on Metronidazole?

People ask this a lot, usually because there's a wedding, a birthday, or a work dinner during their course. The honest answer is that nobody can promise one drink is safe for you. Some people have no reaction at all. Others report feeling sick after a small amount. There's no reliable way to know ahead of time which group you're in, and the label doesn't give a "safe" amount.

If you have an event coming up, some practical options:

- **Ask your doctor about timing.** Sometimes a course can be started a few days earlier or later, or a different treatment can be used. Only your prescriber can decide that, and it's worth asking rather than skipping doses on your own.
- **Have a good alcohol-free option.** Mocktails, alcohol-free spirits (check the label, since some contain traces), sparkling water with lime, or a soda in a wine glass mean you're not standing there empty-handed.
- **Have a simple line ready.** "I'm on antibiotics" is a complete sentence. Nobody needs more detail than that.

## A Note on DHM and Hangover Supplements During Treatment

Because this is a hangover-focused site, people sometimes ask whether a supplement like DHM (dihydromyricetin) could make it safe to drink on metronidazole. It can't. There is no good evidence that DHM, or any other supplement, prevents the reaction described on the metronidazole label, and nothing makes it safe to ignore that warning. There's also very little research on how DHM interacts with metronidazole, so the sensible move is to skip non-essential supplements during your course unless your pharmacist says they're fine.

DHM is a plant compound that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain. Most of that research is in animals, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. Our [DHM and medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about combining it with common medicines.

## The Bottom Line

Metronidazole is a useful antibiotic, and the alcohol warning that comes with it is real enough to respect, even though the science behind it is less clear-cut than most sources suggest. Avoid alcohol from your first dose until at least 72 hours after your last, watch for hidden alcohol in mouthwash, liquid medicines, and food, and finish your whole course even if you slip up. If you accidentally drink, stay calm, watch for symptoms, keep taking your antibiotic, and call your pharmacist. Get emergency help for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or vomiting that won't stop.

Once your treatment is finished and the three days are up, you're back to normal drinking advice: pace yourself, eat first, and alternate with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the basics that work. If you're also curious about painkillers for the morning after, see our guides to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).

If you decide to try DHM on a night out *after* your course and the waiting period are done, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it. Think of it as one possible add-on to sensible drinking, not a shield, and never as a reason to drink while you're on a medicine that says not to.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking metronidazole?**

No. The prescribing information for oral metronidazole (Flagyl) says to avoid alcohol during treatment and for at least three days after your last dose, because the combination has been linked to a reaction with flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, cramps, and a fast heartbeat. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you have questions about your specific course.

**How long after metronidazole can I drink alcohol?**

Wait at least 72 hours (three full days) after your last dose. Metronidazole has a half-life of about eight hours, so most of it is cleared in under two days, and the 72-hour window adds a safety margin. If you have liver disease, ask your doctor, because the drug can stay in your body longer.

**Is the metronidazole and alcohol reaction a myth?**

Not exactly. A small placebo-controlled trial and a review of case reports both found weaker evidence for a true disulfiram-like reaction than was once assumed. But case reports of reactions continue, nobody can predict who will react, and alcohol worsens the drug's own side effects. The official label still says to avoid alcohol, and that's the advice to follow.

**What happens if I accidentally drink on metronidazole?**

Many people feel nothing, but some get flushing, a pounding headache, nausea, vomiting, cramps, or a racing heart, usually starting within minutes to an hour and fading over a few hours. Stop drinking, sip water, rest, and call your pharmacist. Don't skip your next dose. Get emergency care for chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, or vomiting that won't stop.

**Should I skip a dose of metronidazole so I can drink?**

No. Skipping doses or stopping early can let the infection come back and make it harder to treat. It also doesn't make drinking safe, because the drug stays in your system for days. If you have an event coming up, ask your doctor whether the timing of treatment can be adjusted.

**Can I use mouthwash while taking metronidazole?**

Use an alcohol-free mouthwash during your course and for three days after. Many popular mouthwashes contain a lot of alcohol, and there are case reports of reactions after using them on metronidazole. This matters especially if you're being treated for a dental infection.

**Is Flagyl the same as metronidazole?**

Yes. Flagyl is a brand name for metronidazole. Generic metronidazole has the same active drug and the same alcohol warning: no alcohol during treatment and for at least 72 hours after your last dose.

**Can I drink alcohol with metronidazole gel?**

It depends on the type. Skin gels and creams for rosacea are absorbed very little, so a reaction is considered unlikely, though alcohol can trigger rosacea flares. Vaginal metronidazole gel is absorbed more, and product labels generally still advise caution, so it's safest to avoid alcohol during treatment and a few days after. Check with your pharmacist about your specific product.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on metronidazole?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement prevents the reaction on the metronidazole label, and little is known about how DHM interacts with metronidazole. Skip non-essential supplements during your course unless your pharmacist says they're fine, and wait the full 72 hours after your last dose before drinking.
